content: The State Children’s Health Insurance Program (SCHIP) is a federal initiative in the United States designed to provide health insurance coverage for families who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but cannot afford private insurance. This program was established in 1997 to address the increasing number of uninsured children in the country. At the time of its inception, SCHIP represented the most significant expansion of health insurance coverage for children since the creation of Medicaid in the 1960s. The program operates under Title XXI of the Social Security Act and was initially championed by Senator Ted Kennedy in collaboration with then-First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. By the federal fiscal year 2006, SCHIP had provided coverage to approximately 9 million children, with every state having an approved plan. States are granted flexibility in implementing the program and receive enhanced federal matching funds to support their efforts. Some states have obtained Section 1115 demonstration authority to use SCHIP funds to cover additional groups, such as parents of children enrolled in SCHIP and Medicaid, pregnant women, and other adults. However, the program has faced funding shortfalls in several states, and efforts to expand its funding have been met with political controversy, with debates centering on its fiscal implications. In 2007, Congress passed a proposal to reauthorize and expand SCHIP, increasing its funding from an average of $5 billion annually to approximately $12 billion annually over five years. This expansion aimed to extend coverage to over 4 million additional participants by 2012 while phasing out most state expansions that included adults other than pregnant women. However, President George W. Bush vetoed the bill, citing concerns that it would federalize health care and expand SCHIP beyond its original intent. Despite bipartisan support in Congress, the House of Representatives fell short of the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto. SCHIP operates as a partnership between federal and state governments, similar to Medicaid. States have the option to design their SCHIP programs as independent child health programs separate from Medicaid, expand their Medicaid programs using SCHIP funds, or combine these approaches. States with separate child health programs enjoy greater flexibility than Medicaid programs, allowing them to impose cost-sharing, tailor benefit packages, and adjust eligibility and enrollment criteria. However, these programs must adhere to federal regulations and outline their characteristics in state plans. In Ohio, for example, SCHIP funds are used to expand Medicaid eligibility for children in families with incomes above the Medicaid thresholds established in 1996, up to 200% of the federal poverty level. In 2004, this translated to a maximum annual income of $37,700 for a family of four at 200% of the federal poverty guidelines. Other states have similar guidelines, with some being more generous or restrictive in the number of children they allow into the program. SCHIP Medicaid expansion programs typically use the same names as their Medicaid counterparts, while separate child health programs often have distinct names. Some states refer to SCHIP as the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP). Despite SCHIP’s efforts, the number of uninsured children continues to rise, particularly among families who do not qualify for the program. Research has shown that children who lose SCHIP coverage often shift from routine care to more expensive emergency care, ultimately costing states more money. A 2007 analysis by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) found that for every 100 children who gain coverage through SCHIP, private coverage decreases by 25 to 50 children, as state programs often offer better benefits at lower costs than private alternatives. The Cato Institute estimated that the crowding out effect of private insurers by public programs could be as high as 60%. In 2007, bipartisan legislation (H.R. 976) sought to expand SCHIP coverage to over 4 million additional participants by 2012, with a five-year budget increase of $35 billion, bringing total SCHIP spending to $60 billion over that period. The bill proposed funding this expansion through an increase in the federal cigarette tax. However, President Bush vetoed the bill, expressing concerns about its potential to expand SCHIP beyond its original scope. Following the veto, the House of Representatives failed to override it, falling 13 votes short of the required two-thirds majority, despite support from 44 Republicans and 229 Democrats.
